tagline: A letter from Paul to his coworker Timothy in Ephesus on false teaching, worship, church leadership, and the life of God's household.
overview:
First Timothy is a letter of instruction to a younger leader left in charge of a troubled church. Paul has gone on to Macedonia and has asked Timothy to stay in Ephesus, where certain teachers were spreading speculation about myths, genealogies, and the law, forbidding marriage and certain foods, and treating godliness as a way to get rich. The letter tells Timothy how to confront them and, just as important, how the church should live: how it should pray, who may lead it and what kind of people they must be, how it should care for widows and honor its elders, and how rich and poor, slave and free, should conduct themselves.

The letter is practical, but it is not merely administrative. Its practical counsel is threaded with some of the New Testament's most compact confessions of faith: that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners (1:15), that there is one God and one mediator between God and men (2:5), and the hymn-like summary of Christ's work in 3:16. Paul's goal, he says at the start, is love that comes from a pure heart, a clear conscience, and a sincere faith (1:5). Sound teaching matters because it produces that kind of life, and false teaching matters because it destroys it.

First Timothy belongs with 2 Timothy and Titus to a group called the Pastoral Letters, a name used since the eighteenth century because the three are addressed to individuals charged with pastoral oversight. They have shaped the church's thinking about ministry more than almost any other part of the New Testament, and several of their passages, especially 2:8-15 on women and 3:1-13 on overseers and deacons, remain among the most debated in Scripture.
author:
The letter opens with Paul's name (1:1) and contains personal detail about his past as a persecutor (1:12-16) and his travels (1:3). The church received it as Paul's from early on. Polycarp of Smyrna, writing in the first half of the second century, appears to echo it; Irenaeus, around AD 180, quotes it and names Paul as its author; and it is included in the Muratorian list of accepted books, usually dated to the late second century. The second-century teacher Marcion did not include the Pastoral Letters in his collection of Paul's letters, and the early papyrus P46 (around AD 200) does not contain them, though its final pages are missing, so it is uncertain whether they were ever there.

Since the early nineteenth century many scholars have concluded that a later follower of Paul wrote the Pastoral Letters in his name. They point to vocabulary and style that differ from Paul's undisputed letters (words such as godliness and sound teaching are frequent here and rare elsewhere), to a more settled church order with overseers, deacons, and enrolled widows, to a false teaching that some see as closer to second-century movements, and to the difficulty of fitting the letters' travel notes into the story of Acts. On this view the letters are a faithful attempt to apply Paul's legacy to a later generation, following a practice of writing in a revered teacher's name that was known in the ancient world.

Scholars who hold that Paul wrote them answer that differences in vocabulary reflect different subjects and a different kind of letter (written to trusted coworkers rather than to congregations), that the church order described is simple and shows no single bishop over the elders, that the false teaching fits a first-century mix of Jewish speculation and ascetic practice, and that the travels fit a period after Acts ends, if Paul was released from his first Roman imprisonment, as early tradition reports. They also note that the early church rejected letters it knew to be written under a false name. Mediating views hold that Paul used a secretary who was given freedom in wording (some have suggested Luke, who is named as Paul's companion in 2 Timothy 4:11), or, as P. N. Harrison argued in 1921, that genuine fragments of Paul's notes were worked into letters completed later. Evangelical scholarship largely holds to Paul's authorship; a majority of critical scholars do not.
date: If Paul wrote the letter, it most likely comes from the period after his release from house arrest in Rome (Acts 28:30-31), around AD 62 to 64, when he had left Ephesus for Macedonia (1:3). This requires a release and a further period of travel not recorded in Acts; Clement of Rome (around AD 96) says Paul reached the limit of the west, and the fourth-century historian Eusebius reports a release and a second imprisonment. A minority of scholars who accept Paul's authorship try to fit the letter within the Acts period, for example during Paul's years in Ephesus (Acts 19) or soon after, though the details fit awkwardly. Scholars who see the letter as written by a later follower usually date it between about AD 80 and 110, and some later still.
setting:
Ephesus was one of the great cities of the Roman Empire, a port on the west coast of Asia Minor (modern Turkey) and the leading city of the province of Asia. It was famous for its temple of Artemis, one of the wonders of the ancient world, and for magic and religious practice of many kinds. Paul had spent about three years there (Acts 19; 20:31), and a large church had grown up, meeting in households across the city. When he said farewell to its elders, Paul warned that men would arise from among them speaking twisted things to draw disciples after them (Acts 20:29-30). This letter shows that warning coming true.

Timothy came from Lystra in Asia Minor, the son of a Jewish mother who believed and a Greek father (Acts 16:1). He had traveled with Paul since the second missionary trip, had been sent on several delicate errands (1 Corinthians 4:17; 1 Thessalonians 3:2), and is named as co-sender of six of Paul's letters. He was younger than many in the church (4:12) and seems to have been in poor health (5:23). His task in Ephesus was not to found a church but to correct one.
purpose: Paul writes so that Timothy, and the church through him, will know how people ought to conduct themselves in God's household, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and foundation of the truth (3:15). The letter equips Timothy to silence false teachers, to restore order to the church's worship, to see that leaders are chosen for their character, to organize care for widows, to deal fairly with elders who sin, and to warn the rich. It is also personal encouragement to a younger leader: keep your conscience clear, watch your life and your teaching, and do not let anyone despise your youth.
story: Acts tells the story of how the good news spread from Jerusalem to Rome, and Paul's letters to churches show it taking root in cities across the empire. The Pastoral Letters show the next step: the apostolic generation passing responsibility to those who will carry the faith after them. First Timothy stands at that handover. It looks back to the gospel Paul received and forward to a church that must guard the deposit of faith without an apostle on hand. After it comes 2 Timothy, Paul's last letter, written as he faces death, and Titus, a close companion to 1 Timothy addressed to churches on Crete.
christ: At the center of the letter's concern for order stands a person. Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, and Paul counts himself the worst of them (1:15). There is one mediator between God and humanity, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all (2:5-6). The hymn of 3:16 traces his story from his appearing in the flesh to his being taken up in glory, and the letter's closing charge points to his confession before Pontius Pilate and to his coming appearance (6:13-14). Sound teaching, in this letter, is the teaching that agrees with the sound words of our Lord Jesus Christ (6:3); the church's order exists to guard and display the truth about him.
reading: First Timothy is a real letter written to a real person in a particular crisis. Read it as the practical application of the gospel to a specific church, and ask at each point what problem in Ephesus Paul is addressing. The letter is not a complete church manual, and its instructions on widows or slaves assume social institutions very different from ours. Watch for the repeated trustworthy sayings (1:15; 3:1; 4:9), which seem to quote early Christian teaching, and for the contrast between sound, healthy teaching and the diseased speculation of the opponents. Where the letter is contested (on women, on church offices, on authorship), read the arguments of more than one side before settling, and notice that Christians who share the same confession about Christ reach different conclusions.

structure.title: The charge against false teaching
structure.summary: Paul urges Timothy to stay in Ephesus and stop the false teachers, sets the law in its proper place, and recalls the mercy shown to him, the worst of sinners.

structure.title: Order in God's household
structure.summary: Instructions on prayer for all people, on men and women in worship, and on the character required of overseers and deacons, closing with a confession of the mystery of godliness.

structure.title: False asceticism and a faithful minister
structure.summary: Paul exposes teaching that forbids marriage and foods and urges Timothy to train himself for godliness and give himself to Scripture, teaching, and example.

structure.title: Caring for the whole family
structure.summary: How to treat older and younger members, support true widows, honor and discipline elders, and teach slaves.

structure.title: Godliness, money, and the final charge
structure.summary: False teachers treat religion as a way to profit; Paul warns against the love of money, charges Timothy to fight the good fight, and instructs the rich to be generous.

themes.title: Sound teaching and a good conscience
themes.body: The letter speaks of sound, literally healthy, teaching, and sets it against speculation that breeds quarrels. Teaching and life are never separated: false teachers have shipwrecked their faith by rejecting a good conscience (1:19), and Timothy will save himself and his hearers by watching both his life and his doctrine (4:16). Truth, in this letter, is meant to make people well.

themes.title: The church as God's household
themes.body: Paul calls the church God's household (3:15), and the image shapes the whole letter. Leaders must manage their own households well, members are to treat one another as fathers, mothers, brothers, and sisters (5:1-2), and families are to care for their own widows. The church is not a lecture hall or a club but a family under God, with the order and mutual obligations a household requires.

themes.title: Godliness
themes.body: The word translated godliness (eusebeia) appears more often in the Pastoral Letters than anywhere else in the New Testament. It names reverence for God worked out in everyday conduct. The false teachers treat it as a means of gain; Paul answers that godliness with contentment is great gain (6:6) and urges Timothy to train for it as an athlete trains (4:7-8).

themes.title: God the Savior of all people
themes.body: The letter repeatedly calls God Savior and stresses the universal reach of his saving will: he wants everyone to be saved (2:4), Christ gave himself as a ransom for all (2:6), and God is the Savior of everyone, and especially of those who believe (4:10). These verses stand behind the church's prayer for all people, including rulers, and its mission to the nations.

themes.title: Wealth and contentment
themes.body: Money runs through the letter: leaders must be free of the love of money, false teachers seek profit, and the letter's closing section warns that the love of money is the root of all kinds of evil (6:10). Yet Paul does not condemn the rich; he charges them to be rich in good works and to hope in God, who richly provides all things for us to enjoy (6:17).

keyChapters.why: Paul's testimony of mercy to the worst of sinners gives the letter its gospel foundation and sets the tone for how Timothy must oppose false teaching.
Contains the confession of one God and one mediator, and the debated instructions on women in worship.
Sets out the character required of overseers and deacons and names the church the pillar and foundation of the truth, closing with an early Christian hymn.
Defends the goodness of creation against false asceticism and gives Timothy a portrait of faithful ministry.
The New Testament's fullest warning about the love of money, and a charge to fight the good fight of the faith.
